Israel: Eisenkot's camp wants to take the Knesset speakership from a Netanyahu ally this Tuesday, even before forming a government

On Tuesday, November 17, the Knesset, Israel's parliament, votes to replace its speaker Amir Ohana, of Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud, with Matan Kahana, of Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party [1]. 67 lawmakers requested the vote [4]. Talks to form a government, meanwhile, remain stuck [3].
Eisenkot's bloc has enough votes to elect Matan Kahana thanks to the Arab parties; support from the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism party could allow some Arab lawmakers to abstain [3].
The request for a vote was filed by 67 of the 120 members of the newly sworn-in parliament, which forced Amir Ohana to hold it [4].
Matan Kahana is a former air force colonel and a former religious affairs minister; he entered the Knesset in 2019 on the Yamina list and returns in 2026 with Yashar [5].
According to Ynet, Gadi Eisenkot first considered keeping the post for himself, then chose Kahana, at least for the duration of the negotiations [9].

Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich (far right) offered to support Kahana on conditions, including not appointing deputy speakers from parties that do not call Hamas a terrorist organization; Kahana refused [1][6].
On Sunday, November 15, Likud and Yashar met and issued a joint statement calling the meeting “professional,” with no progress [3].
On Monday, November 16, a senior official in Eisenkot's bloc said there was no longer any chance of a unity government, denouncing an “attempted coup” by the Prime Minister's Office [2].
Key takeaway: this vote would give Eisenkot's camp control of parliament, while Netanyahu remains prime minister until a new government is formed [8][1].
If Kahana is elected, Eisenkot's bloc wants to start voting as early as Wednesday to repeal the previous government's judicial overhaul, the one that triggered months of protests [8].

The deadlock lies elsewhere: Eisenkot wants his mandate to lead to a coalition he heads himself, while Netanyahu demands to lead a unity government [3]. During President Isaac Herzog's consultations, Eisenkot received 67 recommendations against 46 for Netanyahu [7].

But a recommendation is not a commitment to govern together: the Arab parties that backed Eisenkot do not promise to join his coalition [7]. He has 28 days, extendable by 14 days, to put together a majority [7].

Whoever controls Israel's parliament has a say over the war in Gaza, Lebanon and relations with Iran. A change of majority can shift Israel's policy in a region that supplies part of the oil Europe buys, and therefore the price at the pump.

Kazakhstan: Tokayev fires his intelligence chief, five days after the arrest of the head of the fund worth 40% of GDP

On Monday, November 16, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev replaced the head of the National Security Committee (KNB), Yermek Sagimbayev, with his deputy Marat Irmenov [3]. The KNB had just arrested the heads of the sovereign wealth fund Samruk-Kazyna, whose assets equal about 40% of GDP, and of the national railways [9].
Marat Irmenov was appointed by decree; a second decree dismissed Yermek Sagimbayev, with no official reason given [3][1].
The new chief had been deputy head of the KNB since October 2025; he has worked in the security services since 1996 and has been a general since 2019 [3].

Yermek Sagimbayev had been appointed in January 2022, during the riots that shook the country [4][2]. Three days before his dismissal, Tokayev had still received him for a briefing on corruption and cybersecurity [4].

On November 11, the KNB's anti-corruption service arrested Nurlan Zhakupov, head of Samruk-Kazyna, and Yelzhas Otynshiyev, head of the railway company KTZ; as of the 12th, no specific charges had been made public [7][8].
Yelzhas Otynshiyev had headed KTZ for only four months; before that, he managed Samruk-Kazyna's strategy and assets [7].
On the day of the appointment, Tokayev met with the KNB leadership and called for reforms of the service and better protection of the country's economic interests [5][3].
Key takeaway: in one week, Kazakhstan's leadership struck both the country's largest state company and the service that led the investigation, without explaining anything [1][3].

Samruk-Kazyna controls a large part of the economy: its assets amount to about 40% of gross domestic product [9]. On November 4, Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov had already criticized its managers for delays in investment projects [7].

The fund says it is cooperating with the authorities and that its activities and projects are continuing as planned; Tokayev also says the arrests will not disrupt its operations [6]. Detention is not a conviction, and the investigation is ongoing [6].
The economic backdrop remains supportive: according to figures released on November 17, Kazakhstan's growth accelerated to 4.5% in January-October [10].

Kazakhstan is a major supplier of oil and uranium to Europe, and France has a strong presence there. When the government suddenly shakes up its sovereign wealth fund and its security services, the foreign companies working there, and their employees, watch closely for what comes next.

Papua New Guinea: Prime Minister Marape stands by Taiwan's expulsion and answers his predecessor, Taipei blames Beijing

Papua New Guinea's Prime Minister James Marape on November 17 hit back at criticism from former Prime Minister Peter O'Neill over the closure of Taiwan's representative office in Port Moresby [1][2]. He cites the “One China” policy, while Taiwan has begun withdrawing all its staff [4].
James Marape says the closure is in line with the “One China” policy his country has long followed, and insists Papua New Guinea remains open to business with Taiwan [2][3].
The decision dates back to July 16: Foreign Minister Justin Tkatchenko had demanded the closure of the Taiwanese office, in the name of the “One China” policy [6][7].
According to ABC, Port Moresby wanted to “reassure” Beijing after signing a treaty with Australia [6]. The Chinese embassy welcomed a “right decision” [7].
Taiwan denounced a “unilateral” decision, announced on November 6 that it would close its office itself, then began withdrawing all its diplomatic and technical staff on November 11 [4].
Taipei says Papua New Guinea owed it one year's written notice, while Port Moresby speaks of an immediate closure; Taiwan's foreign ministry accuses China of being behind the decision [5].
The closure ends Taiwan's agricultural, fisheries and medical missions in the country, as well as a scholarship program, laments a Papua New Guinean writer quoted by the Taipei Times [9].
Key takeaway: while not a complete diplomatic break, the expulsion of the Taiwanese office is a win for Beijing in the Pacific, a region where China and Australia compete for influence [6][8].

Papua New Guinea follows the “One China” policy [7]: the Taiwanese office was not an embassy, but it kept practical cooperation going [9]. According to an analyst quoted by the Indian news agency ANI, the Papua New Guinean government may have faced strong pressure from China, or received economic promises; these claims are unproven [8].
The debate is also domestic: former Prime Minister Peter O'Neill criticizes the decision, and James Marape is answering him publicly [2][3].
Taiwan also retaliated on the economic front by suspending its spot purchases of Papua New Guinean liquefied natural gas (LNG) [5].

The Pacific seems far away, but every country that turns its back on Taiwan strengthens Beijing, where many of the things you buy come from, and the chips in your devices depend on it, since they are mostly made in Taiwan. Rising tension around the island can push their prices up.

Australia: the central bank raised rates to 4.85%, the highest since 2008, but a third of its members feared a sharp downturn in the economy

The minutes of the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), released on Tuesday, November 17, detail the November 3 hike: the cash rate was raised to 4.85% in a six-to-three vote. Those against feared a sharper slowdown as the housing market falls. The Australian dollar is at a ten-month low [1][3][5].
At the November 2-3 meeting, six of the nine board members voted for a quarter-point hike, to 4.85%; three wanted to keep the rate at 4.60% [1].
It is the fifth hike of the year and the highest level since 2008; the decision, made on Melbourne Cup day, takes rates to an 18-year high [8][7].

For the majority, the rate was “not clearly sufficient” given persistent inflation: leaving policy too loose was judged riskier than going too far [3][2]. The RBA expects inflation above 3% until the end of 2027 [9].

The three dissenters pointed to rising unemployment and falling house prices, which could signal a “significantly sharper” slowdown; the minutes note that house prices and new home loans have fallen sharply [3].
The text no longer mentions a further hike [8]. ANZ, CBA and Goldman Sachs now believe the rate has peaked [4].

Before the release, the Australian dollar had fallen for five straight sessions, to below 0.6750 US dollars, its lowest in ten months; it then slipped toward 0.6730, driven mainly by the strength of the US dollar [5][6].
In early Tuesday afternoon, Sydney's ASX 200 index was down 1.2%, at 8,936 points, while Commonwealth Bank (CBA) shares were up 0.2% [10].
Key takeaway: the RBA tightened again, but with a divided board, suggesting the hiking cycle is nearing its end [8][4].

The six-to-three vote is closer than expected. For several commentators, it makes a sixth hike much harder [8]. Governor Michele Bullock nonetheless considers that inflation risks remain tilted to the upside [16].
The minority is watching housing: house prices and new loans falling sharply, household credit growth slowing. One hike too many could turn this slowdown into a slump [3].
Wage figures on Wednesday, then employment data, will show whether the economy is slowing enough. CBA sees the RBA on hold, while judging that a hike remains the main short-term risk [15][4].

If you are going to Australia on a working holiday visa or for a semester of study, an Australian dollar at a ten-month low against the US dollar makes your stay a little cheaper. And the situation shows what variable-rate borrowers go through: each central bank rate hike is passed on almost immediately to their monthly payments.

How it works: a central bank's minutes

A central bank sets the rate at which banks lend money to each other overnight; in Australia, it is the “cash rate” [1]. When it raises it, credit becomes more expensive, people borrow and spend less, which slows prices. After each meeting, the RBA publishes minutes describing the debate: the arguments of each side, without saying who voted for what [3]. Markets read them word for word. Here, the majority judged it more dangerous to tighten too little than too much [2], but the disappearance of any mention of a further hike was read as a signal of a pause [8]. What moves the currency: more expected hikes attract capital, fewer hikes drive it away [6].
Past cases: when Australian rates peaked
March 2008
The RBA raises its rate to 7.25%, effective March 5, to bring inflation back to between 2 and 3% [11]. It is then a 12-year high [12].
The global financial crisis then ushers in eleven years dominated by rate cuts [12].
November 2010
The cash rate is raised to 4.75% on November 5, 2010; the average variable mortgage rate reaches 7.81% [13].
A year later, in December 2011, the rate had already come back down to 4.25% [13].
November 2023
In her first decision as governor, Michele Bullock raises the rate from 4.10% to 4.35%, the 13th hike since May 2022 [17], the highest since 2011 [14].
The 4.85% level reached in 2026 exceeds that post-Covid peak [8].

Copenhagen: FLSmidth plunges 8.9% after the abrupt departure of its CFO, Novo Nordisk regains 2.4% thanks to its future anti-obesity drug

On Monday, November 16, two Danish stocks stood out in Europe: FLSmidth, a mining equipment maker, fell 8.9% after the immediate departure of its chief financial officer amid a strategic disagreement; Novo Nordisk gained 2.4% on new data on CagriSema. The Stoxx 600 lost 0.28% [1][3][8].
FLSmidth announced on November 16 that its CFO, Roland M. Andersen, was leaving the group “with immediate effect”; an interim CFO will be appointed later, pending a permanent successor [2][4].
According to the Danish site Proinvestor, the departure stems from a board decision, and the company says it is solely a disagreement over strategy, without further details [3].
The group says the change affects neither its 2026 guidance nor its financial targets through 2029 [3]. The share closed at 517.50 kroner, down 50.50 kroner [16].
The shock contrasts with the previous week: FLSmidth had jumped 5% after quarterly revenue rose 10% and profitability forecasts were raised [6].

At the ObesityWeek conference in Washington, Novo Nordisk presented an analysis of the REDEFINE 1 trial: patients who responded quickly to treatment (at least 5% of weight lost in 8 weeks) lost on average 25.4% of their weight over 68 weeks, versus 17.8% for the others [7].
Novo specifies that this is an after-the-fact analysis, used to form hypotheses, which should not change medical practice; 79.6% of patients had digestive side effects, versus 39.9% on placebo [7].
The Stoxx 600 fell 0.28%, to 662.31 points, ending five sessions of gains, weighed down by AI-related stocks: ASML lost 2.4% and Siemens Energy 1.8% [1].
Key takeaway: a sudden CFO departure always worries investors, because the CFO vouches for the reliability of the accounts and holds the purse strings [3][5].
The vagueness fuels distrust: FLSmidth talks of a strategic disagreement but does not say what it is. Investors sold first, without waiting for explanations [3][5].

For Novo Nordisk, every piece of data on CagriSema counts. The treatment awaits a decision from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in the fourth quarter of 2026, after an application filed in December 2025 [9].
The Danish group needs it: since late 2024, several disappointing results for this drug and lowered forecasts have sent its share price plunging [10][12][14].

“Obesity stocks” like Novo Nordisk carry a lot of weight in many European funds and savings plans: their swings show up in your savings, even if you have never bought the stock. And the FLSmidth case is a reminder that on the stock market, uncertainty is costly: without an explanation, investors sell first.

How it works: why a CFO's departure makes a stock fall

The chief financial officer signs off on the accounts, prepares forecasts and talks to investors every quarter. When they leave overnight, “with immediate effect” and with no successor, as at FLSmidth [2], the market wonders why. A planned departure, with a replacement already named, is reassuring. An abrupt departure raises fears of a hidden problem: the accounts, the forecasts or a disputed strategy. Here, the company cites only a “disagreement over strategy” and maintains its targets [3], but investors sell first, for lack of more information. This is called an uncertainty premium: as long as the doubt lasts, the stock is worth less [5].
Past cases: Novo Nordisk's stock market roller coaster
December 20, 2024
The first major CagriSema trial shows 22.7% weight loss, below the promised 25%: the share falls about 20% and loses €90 billion in value in one session [10].
Its worst day since 2002: the market punishes what was nonetheless a record result, because it hoped for better [11].
Novo cuts its 2025 sales growth forecast to 8-14%, from 13-21%, and names Mike Doustdar CEO [13]: the share loses about $70 billion in value [12].
Competition from copies of its drugs in the United States and slower market growth weigh on the leader [13].
February 23, 2026
CagriSema fails to do at least as well as tirzepatide, Eli Lilly's rival treatment: Novo shares fall 15% [14].
Against Lilly, every new piece of CagriSema data is now closely watched, which explains the 2.4% rebound on November 16 [8].

Baidu, the “Chinese Google,” falls to its lowest in more than five years in Hong Kong: its advertising slumps 22%, despite soaring AI cloud revenue

On Tuesday, November 17, Baidu shares lost nearly 7% at one point in Hong Kong and hit 70.25 Hong Kong dollars, their lowest in more than five years. In the third quarter, its advertising revenue fell 22%, to 11.9 billion yuan, wiping out the 94% jump in AI cloud [2][3][1].
Baidu's revenue fell 1% year on year, to 30.8 billion yuan, in the third quarter of 2026 [1][2].
Online marketing revenue, the group's historic core business, plunged 22%, to 11.9 billion yuan [2]. According to The Next Web, it is the sixth straight quarter of falling revenue [7].
Conversely, AI cloud infrastructure revenue jumped 94%, to 8.2 billion yuan [1], including +191% for computing power (GPU) rental [8].

Adjusted earnings, 6.78 yuan per American depositary share (ADS), beat the analyst average compiled by LSEG (6.36) [2], but remain well below another consensus, at 8.16 yuan [9]: interpretations differ.
CEO Robin Li says he is pleased that his “AI-first” strategy is delivering “concrete results,” despite “headwinds” in advertising [1].
Baidu has bought back about $373 million of its shares since January and plans to pay its first dividend before the end of the year; its Apollo Go robotaxis operate in 30 cities [8].
At midday, Baidu was down 6.8% and the Hang Seng index 0.8%, at 23,571 points [3]; another reading shows Baidu at 70.85 Hong Kong dollars (−5.9%) [6]. Alibaba also hit a new low [5].
Key takeaway: AI is making money for Baidu, but not yet fast enough to offset the erosion of advertising on its search engine, which long made its fortune [2][7].
Even the new “AI-native” advertising, meant to take over, fell 15%, to 2.4 billion yuan [10]. Robin Li insists Baidu will keep investing heavily in AI [1].
The cloud business, for its part, benefits from Chinese companies' demand for computing power. But its 8.2 billion yuan still weighs less than online advertising [1][2].
Tuesday's drop comes in an already nervous market, following the decline of tech stocks on Wall Street [4]. To keep shareholders, Baidu is relying on share buybacks and a first dividend [8].

If you hold a “China” or “emerging markets” fund, Baidu and Alibaba are often part of it: their fall weighs on its value. And Baidu's story shows a risk that also looms over Google: when you get the answer directly from AI, you no longer click on the ads that funded free search.

How it works: the analyst “consensus”

Before each earnings release, dozens of bank analysts estimate a company's revenue and profit. Data providers such as LSEG average them out: this is the “consensus.” The share rises or falls less on the result itself than on the gap with this expectation. At Baidu, revenue is in line with the LSEG consensus [2]. Earnings per share, however, beat one average (6.36 yuan) [2] but miss another (8.16 yuan) [9]: it all depends on which analysts are counted. In such cases, investors look at the long-term engine, here advertising down 22% [2], rather than the quarterly figure.
Past cases: Baidu, from its Hong Kong listing to its fall
March 2021
Baidu lists in Hong Kong at 252 Hong Kong dollars per share and raises $3.1 billion [11]; the share ends its first session, on March 23, exactly at its offer price [12].
The share is now worth less than a third of that offer price [11][2].
Late March 2021
The collapse of the Archegos fund forces banks to sell giant blocks of shares: Baidu loses up to 33.5% in New York in one week [14] and 23.3% over the month [13].
Chinese tech stocks are very sensitive to forced selling by large investors [14].
March 16, 2023
Unveiling of its chatbot Ernie Bot, with a pre-recorded demonstration: the share falls as much as 10% [16] and closes down 6.4%, at 125.10 Hong Kong dollars [15].
Since then, the share has lost nearly 45% more: the market is waiting for AI to really pay off [15][2].

news.2026-11-17-coree-du-sud-suneung-lun: South Korea: two days before the big national exam, every candidate's glasses will be checked for fear of AI cheating

On Thursday, November 19, South Korea holds the Suneung, the university entrance exam [1]. Proctors will check the glasses of every candidate who wears them before each test, to spot smart glasses [1]. At least one trained proctor will be present in each of the 1,300 exam centers [3].

The authorities admit they do not yet have a complete answer to mini-cameras, proof that exams must adapt quickly to these new tools [4].
French exams face the same challenge: phones, watches and soon smart glasses. What Korea is doing this week gives an idea of the checks that could come to the baccalaureate or competitive exams.
